summary:
Earth Sherlock is a Python and Streamlit tool that turns NASA Giovanni time series into a natural language answer to the following questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and is it significant? 

In the demo page, users can pick a question such as “Is the ground drying out?”, which is associated with a variable from a catalog with simple definitions (temperature, humidity, rainfall, soil moisture, wind, and ozone). 
In the other two pages, the user can analyze one region or compare two by uploading his/her own csv files downloaded from Giovanni with whatever variable and region.

The tool removes the seasonal cycle, estimates the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval, and tests significance with three methods: Mann-Kendall, Mann-Kendall with the Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction, and regression with autocorrelation-robust errors. A trend is called significant only if all three tests agree.
details:
Earth Sherlock is a Streamlit web app that takes a NASA's Giovanni monthly time series and answers four questions: what is changing, where, by how much, and is the change significant. It has three pages: a built-in Demo (Italy vs Philippines vs Finland, 2005-2025), a Single region page, and a Compare two regions page, where users upload their own Giovanni CSVs. The pipeline loads the data, removes the seasonal cycle, estimates the trend per decade with a 95% confidence interval (Theil-Sen), and runs three significance tests. It ends with a plain-language verdict and a plot.

Benefits

Users do not need statistics training to get answers.
A trend counts as significant only if all three tests agree, so results are conservative, and non-significant trends are reported honestly instead of hidden.

Tools and technology

  • Language: Python
  • Interface: Streamlit
  • Analysis: pandas, NumPy, SciPy (Theil-Sen, OLS), pymannkendall (Mann-Kendall, Hamed-Rao), statsmodels (autocorrelation-robust regression), Matplotlib
  • Data: NASA Giovanni (GES DISC), using AIRS, MERRA-2, GLDAS and FLDAS variables
  • Hardware: a MacBook Pro 4
  • Super Intelligence: Claude was used in ask mode to accelerate coding

What is creative

  • The “three tests must agree” rule, with the most conservative p-value deciding the verdict
  • A guided use through everyday questions (“Is it getting warmer?”) instead of variables

Factors I considered

  • Audience: students and the public
  • Scope: with two days of development, I request users to upload their own Giovanni’s CSV exports rather than downloading them in the app
